title: Ogre Tress and the Lost Map
markdown:
Ogre Tress had shoulders broad enough to cradle a whole meadow and hands, strong as ancient oaks, that could lift boulders as easily as a squirrel gathers nuts. He was not the gruff ogre of whispers and old wives’ tales. His spirit was as deep and serene as a mountain lake at dawn; his mind, sharp as the crisp clear air of the highest Sky-Soarer Mountains. This blend of brawn and brightness often surprised those who expected only grunt and grind. Beside him, a constant presence, was Mastiff Ink: a magnificent brindle mastiff, quiet nobility, a solid comfort, a nose that could catch the faintest whisper of wild thyme from leagues away. Ink’s steady gaze and the soft thump of his tail were the gentle anchors in Tress’s thoughtful world.

In the highest village, nestled like a handful of jewels on the mountainside, lived Elder Willowbrook. Her face was a tapestry of kindly wrinkles; her cough sounded like dry leaves skittering across stone. The village, dependent on its precious mountain herbs, needed a special remedy.

“Tress, my dear fellow,” she rasped, her voice a thread of moonlight, “the Lumina Bloom, the one that glows with tears of the moon, is the very balm for this bothersome tickle. It blooms only in the secretive Whispering Dell, a place few venture to, and its time is fleeting as the days grow shorter. Will you, with your good heart and strong arms, fetch it for us?”

Tress, whose promises were as steadfast as the mountain peaks, especially to those who smelled of old books and dried lavender, agreed with a surge of purpose. “It would be my deepest honour, Elder Willowbrook.” A finely drawn map, its edges worn smooth by generations of explorers, was pressed into his large palm.

And so, with a satchel plump with honeyed oatcakes and a reassuring pat for Ink’s noble head, Ogre Tress began his undertaking. The winding paths of the Sky-Soarer Mountains were their grand highway, twisting like sleeping dragons up the vast slopes. They passed hidden tarns that mirrored the sapphire sky with perfect stillness, and journeyed through groves of ancient pines, needles singing a constant hushed melody in the wind. Ink trotted faithfully, nose dancing with a thousand scents, ears swiveling, ever attentive.

The mountains, however, had a playful spirit. A gust snatched at Tress’s hat. Loose stones — rather too deliberately placed — tumbled, forcing a scramble that echoed. Then, where the path narrowed to a thread and the world dropped away, a shaggy remarkably determined mountain goat, eyes like polished obsidian, decided the map looked like a particularly tasty turnip. A bold bleat. A flick of horned head. The parchment fluttered up the slope like a trapped moth.

Tress blinked, astonishment rather than anger. “Well, I never.” Ink offered a questioning whine, one worried thump. “It seems, Ink, our trusty guide has sprouted hooves. Our shortcut has become a runaway.”

The Lumina Bloom was in the Dell, a place Tress knew from hushed stories, not from walking. He remembered a general direction; the exact ravines and mossy slopes had gone hazy, a dream upon waking. A pebble of unease in the boot: he did not like being lost when a solemn promise was at stake.

Ink nudged the calloused hand. Tress took a breath of crisp air. “Perhaps there is another way. Not paper. Instinct. Observation.” He remembered a cryptic hint from the Elder: an old hermit’s cave to the north, rumoured to hold forgotten lore.

Wilder terrain. Cooler air, damp earth, pine. Between two moss-covered boulders like sleeping giants: a cave mouth. Dark. Tress, despite his size, felt the familiar flutter — enclosed spaces were not his favourite; he preferred sky. Elder Willowbrook’s cough, and the villagers’ faces, sent him in. Ink trotted first, tail a slow encouraging wag.

Eyes adjusted. Not a damp earthy hole: a library. Shelves carved from living rock, laden with scrolls and tomes whose bindings held a faint internal light. Aged parchment, dried heather, a hint of honey from forgotten blossoms. And eyes: a small sleek black cat, regal on a teetering stack. Blink. Emerald, two gemstones. The library’s silent guardian. It did not speak. It led them, whiskers twitching, to a large unfurled scroll: the paths they had walked, the Whispering Dell marked by a radiant dew-kissed flower.

Tress smiled, apprehension chased off. The scroll showed more than routes: diagrams of plants, notations of wind, and a small amusing drawing of a goat looking pleased with itself, horns adorned with a stolen scrap of parchment. Tress’s keen mind, and the cat’s silent guidance, pieced it. The goat had likely taken the map toward Sunstone Ridge, famous for succulent emerald mosses. The Bloom, a delicate brushstroke said, favoured shaded crevices on the north-facing side, where cool damp mist lingered longest.

He thanked the silent cat. The guardian simply blinked its emerald eyes, a slow knowing gesture that spoke volumes. Ink gave a happy echoing bark, tail now wagging with unrestrained joy. They followed the clues from the scroll, Tress’s mind sharp and clear, earlier disorientation replaced by a quiet confident resolve. And there, tucked away in a cool mossy crevice, just as the scroll had so precisely promised, they found them: a cluster of Lumina Blooms, each delicate petal shimmering with an ethereal pearly light, as if they had captured starlight and moonlight in their very being.

The journey back was swift and sure. The mountain paths, which had seemed so unhelpful and confusing before, now felt like familiar welcoming friends. Tress carried the precious blooms carefully in his satchel, large hands surprisingly tender, ensuring not a single petal was bruised. He had faced his mild apprehension of enclosed spaces, the frustration of a lost map, and the impudence of a pilfering goat, and he had managed it not with brute force but with cleverness and the dog at his knee.

When he presented the Lumina Blooms to Elder Willowbrook, the faint pearly light of the flowers seemed to glow within her hands. Her cough instantly subsided, replaced by a contented sigh that rippled through the small cottage. The villagers rejoiced, faces alight with relief and gratitude, and Tress, the large gentle ogre, felt a warmth spread through him, a quiet satisfaction better than any honeyed oatcake. He had kept his promise through wit, patience, and the unwavering loyalty of Mastiff Ink. The goat, somewhere on Sunstone Ridge, was presumably still enjoying its turnip of a map. Tress did not mind. The Dell had given what the paper had only pointed toward, and Ink’s tail, thumping on the cottage step, was all the cartography he needed for the walk home.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
